questions.question: Ravi shades a circle that is cut into 6 equal slices. He shades 4 slices. Which picture shows the same fraction shaded?
options: A grid of 12 equal squares with 4 squares shaded
A circle cut into 8 equal slices with 4 slices shaded
A grid of 3 equal columns with 2 columns shaded
A bar cut into 6 equal parts with 3 parts shaded
questions.explain: Ravi shaded 4/6, and 4/6 = 2/3 because both the top and bottom are divided by 2, which matches 2 columns out of 3. The common trap is hunting for a picture with 4 shaded pieces — the number of pieces can change as long as the amount of the whole stays the same.

questions.question: Ben is filling in a fraction wall. He needs a fraction equal to 3/5 that has 20 as its denominator. Which fraction should he write?
questions.explain: To get from 5 to 20 you multiply by 4, so you must multiply the numerator by 4 as well: 3 x 4 = 12, giving 12/20. The common trap is adding 4 to both numbers (7/9) or changing only one of them — adding does not keep the value the same, multiplying does.

questions.question: In class, Ella draws a number line from 0 to 1 and divides it into 8 equal spaces. She puts a dot on the 6th mark after 0. Which fraction lands on exactly the same point as Ella's dot?
questions.explain: The dot is at 6/8, and dividing the top and bottom by 2 gives 3/4, so both fractions mark the same point on the line. The common trap is halving only the numerator (3/8), which moves the dot to a completely different place.

questions.question: Léa wants a $24 ticket for the Science World trip. She has already saved $18. Written in lowest terms, what fraction of the ticket price has she saved?
questions.explain: She has saved 18/24; dividing the top and bottom by the greatest common factor 6 gives 3/4. The common trap is stopping early — dividing by only 2 or only 3 gives 9/12 or 6/8, which are equal in value but are not in lowest terms.

questions.question: Tia and Jonah are reading the same novel. Tia has read 4/6 of the book and Jonah has read 6/9 of it. Have they read the same amount, and how can you tell?
options: No — you cannot get from 4/6 to 6/9 by multiplying, so they must be different.
Yes — 4/6 and 6/9 both simplify to 2/3, so they are equivalent.
No — 6/9 is more because both of its numbers are bigger than the numbers in 4/6.
Yes — you just add 2 to the top and 3 to the bottom, so the fractions keep the same value.
questions.explain: Divide 4/6 by 2 and 6/9 by 3: both become 2/3, so the two readers are at the same point in the book. The common trap is judging by the size of the digits, or by adding a number to the top and bottom — only multiplying or dividing both parts by the same number keeps the value.

questions.question: At the Burnaby block party there are two identical trays of blueberry cake. Tray A is cut into 12 equal pieces and 8 pieces are taken. Tray B is cut into 9 equal pieces and 6 pieces are taken. Which tray has more cake left?
options: Tray A, because 4 pieces are left on Tray A and only 3 pieces are left on Tray B.
Tray B, because ninths are bigger pieces, so 3 big pieces beat 4 small pieces.
Neither — the same amount is left, because 8/12 and 6/9 both equal 2/3 taken, leaving 1/3 of each tray.
Tray A, because 8/12 is a smaller fraction taken than 6/9.
questions.explain: Simplify each amount taken: 8/12 = 2/3 and 6/9 = 2/3, so exactly 1/3 of each identical tray is left. The common trap is counting leftover pieces instead of comparing fractions — 4 pieces and 3 pieces look different, but the pieces are different sizes.

questions.question: Owen says that 2/3 = 5/6 because he added 3 to the top and 3 to the bottom. To check, he draws one number line from 0 to 1 marked in thirds and another marked in sixths, lined up underneath. What do the number lines show?
options: Both dots land on the same point, so Owen is right that 2/3 = 5/6.
2/3 lands past 5/6, because thirds are bigger pieces than sixths.
Owen should have added 3 to the denominator only, so 2/3 = 2/6.
5/6 lands past 2/3: on the sixths line 2/3 matches 4/6, so equivalent fractions come from multiplying the top and bottom, not adding.
questions.explain: Multiplying 2/3 by 2/2 gives 4/6, so 2/3 sits on the 4/6 mark and 5/6 is one sixth further along the line. The most common mistake in this unit is adding the same number to the numerator and denominator — that always changes the value, while multiplying or dividing both by the same number keeps it.
